items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to calculate the integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
At first glance, this looks kind of tricky. However, if we use the identity [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sin x} = \csc x,] we can rewrite the integral as

Content:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(\sin^{2} x)dx = ∫((1)/(\sin x))^{2}dx = ∫\csc^{2} xdx,]

Content:
and we see that this is just a standard trigonometric integral:

Content:
[MATH: \int\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\,\textrm d x = \int\csc^2 x\,\textrm d x =-\cot x + C]

Content:
When confronted with a tricky-looking trigonometric integral, we can often reduce it to a standard integral using a trigonometric identity.

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\left(\cot x + \sin^2 x\right)\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\sin x } = \csc x,] as follows:

[MATH: ∫(1)/(\sin x)(\cot x + \sin^{2} x)dx|= ∫((1)/(\sin x) ⋅ \cot x + (1)/(\sin x) ⋅ \sin^{2} x)dx; = ∫(\csc x ⋅ \cot x + \sin x)dx; = ∫\csc x\cot xdx + ∫\sin xdx; = − \csc x − \cos x + C]

sections.normalized_html:
We can write the integral as

[MATH: \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,\textrm d x = \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,\textrm d x.]

We then use the fact that [MATH: \dfrac{\sin x }{\cos x} = \tan x] and [MATH: \dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x] to express this as

[MATH: \int_0^{\pi/3} \sec x\tan x\,\textrm d x,]

which is a standard trigonometric integral. Therefore,

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{π/3}(\sin x)/(\cos^{2} x)dx|= ∫_{0}^{π/3}\sec x\tan xdx; = \sec x|_{0}^{π/3}; = \sec ((π)/(3)) − \sec (0); = 2 − 1; = 1.]

items.title: Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution

sections.normalized_html:
We use the identity [MATH: \tan 2x = \dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}] and rewrite the integral as

[MATH: \int \tan{2x}\,\textrm d x = \int \dfrac{\sin{2x}}{\cos 2x}\,\textrm d x.]

Notice that the numerator of the integrand is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we can solve this by substitution.

Let [MATH: u=\cos 2x.] Then

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-2 \sin 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac 1 2 \,\textrm d u= \sin 2x \, \textrm d x.]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of [MATH: u] and evaluate:

[MATH: ∫(\sin 2x)/(\cos 2x)dx|= − (1)/(2)∫(1)/(u)du; = − (1)/(2)\ln|u|+ C; = − (1)/(2)\ln|\cos 2x|+ C; = (1)/(2)\ln|(\cos 2x)^{− 1}|+ C; = (1)/(2)\ln|\sec 2x|+ C]
